quote_item6: Our methodology describes “junk news” as sources that meet three out of the following five criteria: (1) professionalism, where sources fall short of the standards of professional journalistic practice including information about authors, editors, and owners; (2) style, where inflammatory language, suggestion, ad hominem attacks and misleading visuals are used; (3) credibility, where sources report on unsubstantiated claims, rely on conspiratorial and dubious sources, and do not post corrections; (4) bias, where reporting is highly biased and ideologically skewed and opinion is presented as fact; and (5) counterfeit, where sources mimic established news publications in branding, design, and content presentation.
quote_item10: The largest proportion of content being shared by Twitter users interested in UK politics comes from Professional News Sources, which account for 48.8% of all content. In comparison, Junk News and Information account for 10.3% of all content shared.
notes: Neudert, Howard & Kollanyi 2019 (Social Media + Society), FR/UK/DE elections. Item1/2 HIGH: frame is manually chosen election hashtags on Twitter, generalised to 'voters'; hashtag-seeded, and Twitter users are not the electorate. Item3 LOW: Streaming API collection plus a random 10% sample of tweets for coding. Items 4/5 NA (source-level content analysis of shared URLs). Item6 HIGH: 3-of-5 source-level criteria in which bias, style and professionalism (quality/partisanship) can alone satisfy the threshold without any falsity determination - the CONTENT-vs-QUALITY failure. Item7 LOW: Krippendorff's alpha = .89 reported, 22 months of iterative codebook development; caveat that the alpha comes from the shared English/US dataset and 'We did not calculate intercoder reliability scores within the language-specific teams'. Item8/9 LOW: same API, same typology; dated 7-10 day campaign windows per country. Item10 HIGH: denominator is all classified URLs shared under election hashtags (a political-hashtag subset), not any audience's news or media diet.

quote_item6: Junk news satisfies at least three out of the five following criteria: (1) professionalism, (2) style, (3) credibility, (4) bias, and (5) counterfeit. Our coding decisions encapsulate the content of the domain as a whole (i.e., style, bias, credibility), information about authors and the organization (i.e., professionalism), and the layout and design of the domain itself (i.e., counterfeit).
quote_item10: What are the salient qualities of political news and information shared over social media and how much of the content purporting to be political news and information during the two events was junk news? Based on our grounded typology, Table 2 breaks down the categorical proportions and total counts of sources that citizens shared on Twitter. [Table 2 row: Junk News and Information 486,446 = 17.4%; 21,071 = 18.1%]
notes: Bradshaw, Howard, Kollanyi & Neudert 2019 (Political Communication), US 2016 election + 2018 SOTU. Same Oxford/COMPROP design as 2-s2.0-85074511992. Item1/2 HIGH: manually selected political hashtags, streaming API capped at ~1% of matching public tweets, representativeness explicitly acknowledged as contested. Item3 LOW: full streaming collection of matching tweets; reliability sets drawn as random 50-source samples. Items 4/5 NA. Item6 HIGH: bias/style/professionalism can supply the 3-of-5 threshold with no falsity check; 710 sources coded at domain level only. Item7 LOW: Krippendorff's alpha = 0.89 on the US dataset actually analysed here (stronger than the European companion paper), with disputed cases arbitrated in team meetings. Item8/9 LOW: single instrument, dated windows (1-9 Nov 2016; 24-30 Jan 2018). Item10 HIGH: denominator is 2,792,760 URLs shared under political hashtags, including buckets such as video/image sharing and shopping - a hashtag-defined conversation, not an audience diet. The 17.4% therefore cannot be read as population exposure.

quote_item6: We manually categorized posts into the four types of false narratives: All posts that made a direct claim that Black Panther was Alt-Right through words or images were categorized as Alt-Right. All posts that made a claim of a scene occurring in the movie that did not occur were labeled as Fake Scene.

notes: Ng, Robertson et al. (ACM JDIQ 2019), #BlackPanther. Item1/2 HIGH: single-hashtag, single-film conversation over 16 days; the false-narrative numerator was seeded from 15 Buzzfeed/Vox news articles and then keyword-expanded, so both frame and numerator are journalism-curated. Item7 HIGH: no kappa/alpha, no validated instrument, manual categorisation by the authors. Item9 LOW: 8-23 Feb 2018 stated and event-appropriate. This analysis was based on a manual from the Brazilian news portal G1']

[EN: 'After receiving and organising the data from each group, the shared multimedia contents - text, still image, video, link, pdf and audio - corresponding to political topics were selected, giving a sample of 472 posts.']

Item1/2/3 HIGH: 10 family groups recruited by an open call posted on Facebook/WhatsApp; pure convenience. Item1 LOW: target population is US adults 18+, survey-weighted, benchmarked against the 2016 ANES face-to-face survey on demographics and turnout (56.6% recorded turnout vs 54.7% national). Item6 HIGH: 'imprecisões clínicas/científicas' is physician-judged accuracy/quality coding, not external falsity ground truth. Item10 HIGH: denominator = 242 keyword-retrieved topical videos.

quote_item6: Our measure of untrustworthy website exposure was calculated using a list of 668 untrustworthy websites created by Allcott et al., (2019). Their list, which is the most expansive to date, was created by combining five existing lists of untrustworthy sites previously gathered by researchers, journalists, and fact-checking sites
quote_item10: 671 respondents with both survey data and acceptable browsing histories ... visits to these untrustworthy websites were very rare; 60.8% of respondents visited zero sites and 95.6% visited four or less.
notes: Best-in-shard on the load-bearing items. Item6 LOW: pre-existing, externally compiled 668-site untrustworthy domain list (the instrument's 'validated domain/credibility list'). Item10 LOW: denominator is the whole 90-day desktop browsing diet of 671 real US adults (>15M visits), i.e. a real audience denominator, not a curated topical corpus. Item5 LOW: complete behavioural trace collected with consent. Item3 HIGH: 'The recruitment strategy is limited in that it does not produce a probability based sample'. Item4 HIGH: opt-in Facebook-ad recruitment plus browsing-data donation; funnel reported (3735 clicks -> 764 surveys -> 736 uploads -> 671 retained) and composition skewed (74.5% women, 78.7% White) with no weighting. Known undercoverage of mobile/in-app visits noted by the authors but mode is consistent across subjects (item8 LOW).

quote_item6: We use Google Fact Check Explorer via its API to extract a baseline dataset of all English language misinformation related to COVID-19 from March 2020 (that had a claim or review date between the 1st and 31st of March) ... This dataset includes 247 debunked stories, and after removing duplicates 226 debunked stories remained.
quote_item10: The selected tweets together with copies (that were excluded for further analysis) made up 29% of the manually assessed tweets, and roughly extrapolating would mean that about 100,000 of the nearly 17.5 million tweets were related to misinformation that we captured.
notes: Items 4/5 NA (content analysis). Item6 LOW: fact-checker ground truth (226 Google Fact Check Explorer debunked claims), the strongest case definition in this shard. Item7 LOW: keyword classifiers validated by manual coding of a random 100 tweets per classifier, Krippendorff alpha = 0.74 reported for story typing. Item3 LOW: full census of the hashtag stream plus random subsets for manual validation. Items 1-2 HIGH: universe is 76 COVID-19 hashtags, a keyword-seeded topical corpus, yet the claim generalises ('the amount of misinformation shared on Twitter is very small'). Item10 HIGH: 17.5M COVID-hashtag tweets is a curated topical denominator, and the 0.6% numerator is an explicitly 'rough' extrapolation from manually assessed subsets that only captures already-fact-checked claims.

quote_item6: In order to measure exposure to vaccine-related misinformation, we asked respondents whether they encountered each of eight common misinformation themes in the previous 6 months. Misinformation themes were identified based on an academic literature review, as well as current public health guidance.
quote_item10: High levels of misinformation exposure were observed among participants, with 73% reporting some exposure to misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines in the past 6 months
notes: Item1/item2 LOW: real public (Florida adults) reached through a quota-matched commercial web panel benchmarked to Census and state demographics. Item10 LOW: denominator is the 600 surveyed adults, a genuine population denominator. Item6 LOW: the eight themes are externally identified falsehoods (CDC-flagged), not author-devised quality judgements. Item3 HIGH: stratified quota sampling from an opt-in panel, not probability selection. Item4 HIGH: no response or attrition rate reported; authors note under-representation of those without a high-school degree and of rural residents. Item7 HIGH: self-report recall instrument with no validation or reliability evidence, and the authors themselves call it 'a strong proxy measure for overall misinformation exposure' - self-reported recall over 6 months is the dominant bias here, likely upward.

quote_item6: Respondents were asked if they had ever seen claims that 'smoking/alcohol drinking can protect against COVID-19' from WhatsApp/WeChat, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and online forums (including Telegram).
quote_item10: Of the 1501 respondents, 282 (19.0%; 95% CI 16.8% to 21.4%) reported having seen claims that 'smoking/alcohol drinking can protect against COVID-19' from social networking sites.
notes: Luk et al., Tob Control 2020, Hong Kong. Population-based RDD landline + representative mobile panel; response rates reported (61.3% landline, 61.7% mobile) and prevalence weighted by sex/age/education -> items 1-4 LOW. Item 6 LOW: the claim is a specific, externally adjudicated falsehood (WHO explicitly warned there is no evidence); a single named false claim rather than author-devised subjective coding. Item 7 HIGH: exposure measured by a single unvalidated self-report item, no reliability statistic (cognitive interviewing with 10 people was for questionnaire refinement only); recall exposure is known to be poorly calibrated. Item 8 LOW despite mixed CATI/web modes because survey method was adjusted for and was not associated with exposure. Item 10 LOW: denominator is the full weighted population sample (1501), numerator is respondents reporting exposure - a true population-level prevalence, though of one specific claim only, not of misinformation in general.

quote_item6: The list of fake news sites was composed of the 624 websites that had been previously identified by researchers, professional fact-checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news.
quote_item10: Following this procedure, we found that 2.5% of clicks were to fake news, 24% of clicks were to not-fake news, and 74% of clicks were to not-news sites (shown in Column A in Table 1).
notes: Allen, Mobius, Rothschild & Watts (HKS Misinfo Review) - a methodological critique of the Facebook URLs dataset. Item 10 LOW and the exemplar case for the review: the Nielsen denominator is ALL clicks from the Facebook newsfeed including not-news (74%), i.e. a whole-diet denominator, and the paper's entire point is that the censored Facebook URLs frame (100+ public shares) inflates fake news 4X. The 12% estimate is presented explicitly as the biased comparator, not as the authors' preferred prevalence. Item 6 LOW under the instrument's 'validated domain/credibility list' rule (Allen et al. 2020 list, external, from fact-checkers/journalists) - but note the list blends 'low-quality' and 'hyperpartisan' with 'fake', so it is a source-quality proxy, not claim-level falsity. Item 7 LOW: pre-existing published domain list = validated instrument. Item 4 UNCLEAR: Nielsen panel opt-in/consent bias not quantified; desktop-only coverage is acknowledged as a limitation but not corrected, which matters given Facebook use is mostly mobile.

quote_item6: In this study, we focus on one particular myth (and its language variants) related to MOUD: agonist therapy or medication-assisted treatment (MAT) is simply replacing one drug with another.
quote_item10: Platform-level prevalence was calculated thereafter by machine labeling all unannotated posts with the classifier and noting the proportion of myth-indicative posts over all posts.
notes: ElSherief et al., JMIR 2021. Items 1-2 HIGH: the universe is a 152-keyword opioid lexicon corpus plus 22 opioid-specific subreddits - an artificial, topic-curated frame, not any audience. Item 3 LOW: full census of the collected frame (all posts machine-labelled; 6,365,245 tweets). Items 4-5 NA (pure content analysis). Item 6 LOW: a single, clinically discredited claim with explicit external ground truth in the clinical literature, annotated by public-health experts. Item 7 LOW: classifier validated (91% accuracy, AUC 0.9) on expert annotations - but note all myth-KNN posts were annotated by ONE expert annotator, so no inter-annotator reliability is available. Item 8 HIGH: collection mode differed by platform (11 keywords in video titles for YouTube vs the full 152-keyword lexicon for Reddit/Drugs-Forum vs all-tweet querying for Twitter) and platform prevalences are compared directly. Item 9 LOW: window stated (1 Jan 2018 - 31 Dec 2019). Item 10 HIGH: denominator is a keyword-curated topical corpus, numerator is one single myth, and the 0.4-0.9% is reported as 'prevalence' - it is a within-topic content rate, not audience exposure.

quote_item6: Moreover, in the present study 3 (6%) misleading videos were detected (defining NIPT as a diagnostic test).
quote_item10: The first 50 most viewed were analyzed after exclusion of videos with a non-English language (n=4), videos repeated twice (n=3), irrelevant video (n=1), and the sources other than our study groups (foundation/advocacy group, celebrity/public figure/influencer, etc.) (n=2).
notes: Yener & Ates, Eurasian J Fam Med 2021. Items 1-3 HIGH: single keyword search ('Non-invasive prenatal testing') sorted by view count, top 50 retained - a purposive, topic-curated, top-N frame, not an audience. Items 4-5 NA (content analysis). Item 6 HIGH: no a priori operational definition of misinformation is given; the 9-item dichotomous questionnaire measures whether common questions are ANSWERED, and the misinformation judgement is the two obstetricians' post hoc reading (only characterised retrospectively in the Discussion as 'defining NIPT as a diagnostic test'). Item 7 HIGH: no kappa or any reliability statistic; disagreements handled by informal re-evaluation ('In case of inconsistency, the videos were re-evaluated'). The validated tools used (GQS, PEMAT-A/V, JAMA benchmarks) measure QUALITY, not falsity - the CONTENT-vs-QUALITY conflation this review targets. Item 9 HIGH: single-day snapshot (1 May 2021), acknowledged by the authors as a limitation. Item 10 HIGH: 3/50 curated top-viewed videos, unweighted by the very skewed view counts (13,068 +/- 38,974 per video), presented as the misinformation rate.

quote_item6: Tambien se pregunto si las personas compartieron noticias que consideraban falsas.
quote_item10: En el caso de redes sociales, 81% afirmo no haberlo hecho y 19%, si.
notes: Brenes, Perez & Siles, Cuadernos.info 2022, Costa Rica. English translations of the quotes: item 6 = 'People were also asked whether they had shared news that they considered false.'; item 10 = 'In the case of social media, 81% said they had not done so, and 19% said they had.' Items 1-3 LOW: stratified random sample from the SUTEL national telephone numbering plan, quotas by province/sex/age, education weighted, sampling error +/-3.45pp. Item 4 HIGH: no response, refusal or cooperation rate is reported anywhere. Item 6 HIGH and load-bearing: although the paper gives a rigorous THEORETICAL definition of noticias falsas (Egelhofer & Lecheler's three features - low facticity, news form, intent to deceive), the MEASURE is the respondent's own subjective verdict ('noticias que consideraban falsas' / 'noticias que no son completamente verdaderas'), with no external ground truth whatsoever. Item 7 HIGH: Cronbach alphas are reported for the RWA/SDO/NFC scales but the fake-news exposure and sharing measures are single unvalidated self-report items. Item 9 HIGH: no recall window is specified for the sharing item. Item 10 LOW: denominator is the full representative sample of 805 adults. NB the extracted estimates are self-reported SHARING, which is a weaker proxy for exposure than the paper's frequency-of-encountering items.

quote_item6: Misinformation Yes = if the message contains egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19.
quote_item10: We generated a stratified sample of 3000 posts by randomly selecting 200 posts from each COVID-19 dataset for each credibility category (More, Less, Not Credible, Unrated) and a set of 200 'in platform' posts (i.e., those linking to Twitter from Twitter or Facebook from Facebook).
notes: Broniatowski et al., PLOS ONE 2022. Items 1-2 HIGH: universe is English-language keyword-matched COVID-19 and other-health posts from Twitter and Facebook Pages - a topic-curated content frame, not an audience. Item 3 LOW: stratified RANDOM sampling within the frame. Items 4-5 NA. Item 6 LOW: the extracted estimates come from the human-coded false-claims measure with an explicit written codebook anchored on 'egregious falsehoods', not from the paper's source-credibility proxy - had the credibility proxy been the extracted quantity this would be HIGH (source quality standing in for falsity). Item 7 LOW: three annotators, Krippendorff alpha = 0.742 then 0.811. Item 8 LOW: identical codebook, identical period, equal strata drawn from each platform. Item 9 LOW: window stated (8 March - 1 May 2020, with the matched 2019 comparator). Item 10 HIGH: the denominators are equal-n credibility strata (200 posts per cell) drawn from a keyword corpus, so the 5.17-8.50% figures are within-stratum content rates in a deliberately non-proportional sample - they cannot be read as the prevalence of misinformation in anyone's feed.

quote_item6: Coders were instructed to determine the presence of potential misinformation based on the current literature from peer-reviewed scientific journals or reputable governmental or health agencies, such as the Centers for Disease Control & Prevention, at the time of the tweet.
quote_item10: Of tweets coded as presenting information, 41.7% (n=377) contained at least one piece of potential misinformation, meaning that they were coded as containing anti-vaping exaggeration, pro-vaping exaggeration, statements indicating that nicotine is not addictive or is never harmful, and/or statements indicating that nicotine has unproven health benefits.
notes: Sidani et al., Subst Use Misuse. Items 1-2 HIGH: doubly keyword-filtered frame (JUUL*/vape*/ecig* then nicotine*/addict*) - a topical content universe, no audience. Item 3 LOW: simple random 2% subsample (n=3,116) of the unique-tweet frame. Items 4-5 NA. Item 6 LOW on the instrument's letter - coding is explicitly anchored to peer-reviewed literature and CDC guidance contemporaneous with the tweet, and time-sensitivity is handled carefully (the EVALI example). CAVEAT worth flagging in the write-up: two of the four categories are 'anti-vaping exaggeration' and 'pro-vaping exaggeration', which are claim-strength/framing judgements rather than falsity verdicts, and the authors themselves hedge throughout with 'potential misinformation'; a stricter reading of the CONTENT-vs-QUALITY rule would make this HIGH. Item 7 LOW: two experienced coders, six iterative rounds, Cohen's kappa reported. Item 9 LOW: April 2018 - March 2019. Item 10 HIGH: the denominator is 904 tweets that coders judged to be 'presenting information' - a third filter on top of two keyword filters. Against the coded subsample the figure is 377/3,116 = 12.1% (377/2,943 = 12.8% of ENDS-relevant tweets), so the headline 41.7% is roughly 3.5x inflated relative to even the topical corpus.

quote_item6: Corroborating these claims with fact-checked information from credible sources, including the World Health Organization (WHO)'s Mythbusters [23] and the International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN)'s #CoronaVirusFacts Alliance database [24], we arrived at the following list of 11 false claims:
quote_item10: Drugs and Weather are the two most popular claims, with an average of 84.2% and 77.1% of participants encountering these rumors, respectively
notes: 40-country COVID-19 infodemic survey, PLOS ONE 2022. Item 1 LOW: target is the general public of 40 countries. Item 2 HIGH: the frame is Facebook users who saw and clicked a survey advertisement - the authors concede 'Facebook users are still not demographically representative of countries' populations'. Item 3 HIGH: no random selection; ad-targeting plus self-selection, mitigated only post hoc by raking. Item 4 HIGH: of 44,239 who clicked and began, only 18,314 complete responses were retained (~59% loss); no response rate is computable from ad impressions and drop-out is not characterised. Item 6 LOW and a strength of the study: 11 claims drawn from a physician rumour list and each independently corroborated as false against WHO Mythbusters and the IFCN #CoronaVirusFacts database. Item 7 HIGH: exposure is a single 'have you ever seen this claim' self-report item, unvalidated, with acknowledged social-desirability and question-order concerns. Item 10 LOW: numerator = respondents recalling the claim, denominator = all weighted respondents; a genuine population-share denominator. DISCREPANCY worth noting: the abstract and Fig 1 give 18,407 participants while the Methods report a final dataset of N = 18,314 - the extraction uses 18,407.

quote_item6: Most participants received speculative information on [protection from COVID-19,] for example, the use of chloroquine, hot water, bleach, and herbal remedies.
quote_item10: Overall, 93.1% (1049/1127) received misinformation about the pandemic through social media, and 82.9% (934/1127) believed social media was the primary source of inaccurate information.
notes: Ekezie & Ekezie, Population Medicine 2021, Nigeria. WARNING on the item-6 quote: the cached text is a two-column PDF extraction with interleaved columns; the contiguous verbatim fragment is 'Most participants received speculative information on' ... 'for example, the use of chloroquine, hot water, bleach, and herbal remedies.' The bracketed span is my reconstruction of the broken column and is NOT verbatim - treat only the two fragments as quoted text. Item 6 HIGH: the paper contains NO operational definition of misinformation anywhere - respondents self-classified what they had 'received' as misinformation, with the four exemplars above supplied only in the Results narrative; there is no fact-check anchor, claim list, or coding scheme. Item 2 HIGH: snowball recruitment via email and social networks; the achieved sample is 92.1% educated to undergraduate level or above, which is wildly unrepresentative of Nigerian adults; the authors concede 'the online recruitment strategy may have limited respondent variety'. Item 3 HIGH: snowball/convenience, no random selection. Item 4 HIGH: no response rate, no denominator of invitees, no weighting. Item 7 HIGH: single unvalidated self-report item, no reliability. Item 9 LOW: fielded June 2020, stated. Item 10 LOW on construction (1049/1127 = the whole achieved sample) - the problem here is the sample itself (items 2-4), not the fraction. Note this sits at the MODERATE/HIGH border: 5 HIGH items with item 6 HIGH; only item 10 being LOW keeps it out of HIGH.

quote_item6: Videos were classified as misleading if it contained information lacking scientific evidence (e.g., unsubstantiated claims about treating ADHD).
quote_item10: Of the 100 videos meeting inclusion criteria, 52% (n = 52) were classified as misleading, 27% (n = 27) as personal experience, and 21% (n = 21) as useful.
notes: Yeung et al., Can J Psychiatry 2022, TikTok #adhd. Items 1-3 HIGH: single hashtag query, TikTok's proprietary popularity algorithm, sorted descending by view count until 100 videos were reached - purposive top-N on a curated topical universe. Items 4-5 NA. Item 6 HIGH and squarely the falsity-vs-quality problem: 'misleading' is defined as information LACKING scientific evidence and adjudicated against CADDRA and AAP practice guidelines - i.e. guideline non-adherence and absence of evidence standing in for falsity, exactly the substitution the instrument flags. It is aggravated by the rule that a personal-experience video containing 'any generalized misleading statements' is reclassified as misleading, which pulls anecdote into the numerator. Item 7 LOW: two clinician raters, 86% agreement, kappa 0.7766, third-rater adjudication. Item 9 HIGH: single-day query (18 July 2021) generalised to a prevalence claim about ADHD content on TikTok. Item 10 HIGH: 52/100 top-viewed videos, unweighted by views despite a 892,100-14,800,000 view range across the sample, and set against 4.3 billion #adhd views overall - the 52% is a rate within a hand-sized curated set, not a share of what viewers see. Both items 6 and 10 HIGH -> overall HIGH by the pre-specified rule (n_high = 6 independently also gives HIGH).

quote_item6: Videos were considered non-factual if they contained one or more non-factual statements, defined as contradictory to guidelines published by public health agencies (ie, WHO or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) at the time of video publication.
quote_item10: Of 150 videos screened, 122 videos (81%) were included.
notes: Top-150-by-views YouTube search for 'COVID-19 vaccine' on a single day (21 July 2021); items 1-3 HIGH (topical, keyword-seeded, top-N-by-engagement frame). Item 6 LOW: falsity assessed statement-by-statement against a named external reference standard (WHO/CDC), coded in duplicate with third-reviewer consensus. Item 7 HIGH: no kappa or other reliability statistic for the factual/non-factual coding (mDISCERN/mJAMA are validated quality scales, not falsity instruments). Item 9 HIGH: single-day search snapshot, no publication window on the sampled videos, generalised to 'YouTube as a source of misinformation'. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 122 curated top-viewed topical videos; the 11% view-weighted figure uses publisher-side view counts, not an audience diet. Quotes reassembled across two-column interleaving in the cached text; wording verbatim.

quote_item6: Judgments of possible medical misinformation were submitted to a public health expert for verification.
quote_item10: we were able to catalog data for 1672 web pages about vaccination in the U.S.
notes: One of the stronger designs in the shard. Item 6 LOW: explicitly conservative, narrowly medical case definition, independently verified by a public-health expert (107 candidates -> 56 confirmed); financial/religious claims deliberately excluded. Item 7 LOW: two independent coders, consensus resolution, conditional IRR and absolute agreement reported (though the reported reliability figures cover gist/narrative/emotional appeal rather than the misinformation judgement itself - expert verification carries the validity claim). Item 8 LOW: identical manual cataloguing protocol; multiple search engines/states were a deliberate coverage strategy, not an unadjusted mode difference. Item 9 LOW: 2020 collection window stated. Items 1-3 HIGH: alphabet-spanning keyword-seeded Google frame, 5 results pages deep, purposive. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 1672 catalogued vaccination web pages (a curated topical corpus), not any audience's information diet.

quote_item6: confirmed that all of the 8 popular rumors in Textbox S1 in Multimedia Appendix 1 are false, while the narratives of the 11 food scandals in Textbox S2 in Multimedia Appendix 1 reflect the facts in 2016, though 2 of them are not accurate.
quote_item10: Among the respondents, 83.6% (2584/3090) heard at least one food rumor.
notes: Only genuine population-denominator study in the shard. Items 1-3 LOW: multistage stratified door-to-door probability sample of adults in Beijing and Hefei (real public, not an artificial universe); not national, but the adapted rule targets artificial universes. Item 5 LOW: direct survey of subjects. Item 6 LOW: eight pre-specified rumours verified false against official state surveillance sources - external ground truth, though the verifying sources (People's Daily Online, Xinhuanet) are state-controlled, so independence is not assured. Item 4 HIGH: the reported 'response rate was 42.65% for Beijing and 57.35% for Hefei (out of 3090 participants)' is a sample split, not a response rate; true non-response/attrition is not reported. Item 7 HIGH: dichotomous self-reported yes/no recall items, no validity or reliability evidence. Item 9 HIGH: no recall window stated for 'having heard' a rumour (unbounded), while media-use items used a 12-month frame. Item 10 LOW: denominator is the 3090 surveyed adults, but note 2584 is also given as the number of valid questionnaires after list-wise deletion - a possible numerator/denominator reporting error worth flagging in the review.

quote_item6: we refer to social media posts that make claims and put forward verifiably untrue speculations according to our analysis using a pre-trained BERT classifier.
quote_item10: Overall, the classifier categorized about 21% of the comments and 15% of the replies as fake
notes: Items 1-2 HIGH: four purposively chosen channels (CNN, Fox News, The Epoch Times, WHO) and keyword-matched videos - an artificial universe assembled to span partisanship, not an audience. Item 3 LOW: complete API census of all comments on the 1565 videos. Item 6 HIGH: the case definition is self-referential ('according to our analysis using a pre-trained BERT classifier') and the classifier was trained on 11,771 fact-check-tagged news/social posts (Patwa et al.) then transferred to YouTube comments, a different genre where much of the text is opinion rather than checkable claim; a 21% falsity rate over all comments reflects that domain shift. Item 7 LOW: precision 0.93 / recall 0.86 / F1 0.89 and 91% accuracy reported, but on a held-out split of the training distribution, not on labelled YouTube comments. Item 9 LOW: 16-month window (11 Mar 2020 - 29 Jul 2021) stated. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is ~2.5M comments on a curated topical video set. Items 6 and 10 both HIGH -> overall HIGH.

quote_item6: if they attempted to link the death of Hank Aaron with administration of the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine.
quote_item10: A total of 436 tweets were initially sampled from the Twitter Search Application Programming Interface.
notes: Single-event, keyword-defined corpus ('Hank Aaron' + 'vaccine'). Items 1-2 HIGH: the universe exists only because of the misinformation event. Item 3 HIGH: Twitter Search API v1.1 returns 'recent and popular' tweets, so retrieval is neither random nor a complete census, and a snowball 'Seeded Sample' was layered on top. Item 6 HIGH: misinformation is coded by topical linkage ('attempted to link the death ... with administration of the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine') rather than against a fact-check verdict, so assertion, questioning and mention are conflated; the WHO SAGE matrix used is a hesitancy framework, not a truth standard. Item 7 LOW: kappa=0.83 reported for misinformation codes with discrepancy reconciliation. Item 9 LOW: 7-day window justified by circaseptan sentiment literature. Item 10 HIGH: 56% is 244/436 tweets about one death, presented as vaccine-misinformation prevalence.

quote_item6: videos were tagged as misleading if they included information that vitamin D prevents or cures COVID-19, which is a statement that is not in line with the current evidence base, which presently only concludes a correlation between the 2
quote_item10: In total, 77 (64.2%) of 120 YouTube videos screened were included in our analysis.
notes: Highest n_high in the shard (7). Items 1-3 HIGH: first 60 YouTube search results for 'COVID'/'coronavirus'/'vitamin D' at two timepoints, screened to 77. Item 6 HIGH: the coding pair is 'useful (all accurate information)' vs 'misleading (any inaccurate or misleading content)' - a quality/accuracy continuum standing in for falsity, and the 7 videos containing a mix of useful and misleading content were labelled misleading overall, inflating the 80.5% figure. Item 7 HIGH: a priori codebook and two coders with senior-author adjudication, but no kappa or other reliability statistic. Item 9 HIGH: two single-day search snapshots (10 Jun and 7 Dec 2020) generalised to platform-level prevalence. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 77 doubly-topical videos (COVID AND vitamin D).

quote_item6: The categorization of articles involved a narrow and dichotomous analysis of accuracy to determine whether something was or was not misinformation.
quote_item10: The top 10 articles for each keyword were included in the analysis.
notes: The 0% estimate is an artefact of an extremely narrow denominator, and this appraisal should carry that. Items 1-3 HIGH: BuzzSumo top-10-by-total-engagement per keyword per week, two keywords, six weeks = 120 articles; explicit top-N-by-engagement selection. Item 6 HIGH: no substantive case definition is given beyond a 'narrow and dichotomous analysis of accuracy'; no external ground truth, no fact-check source, no worked criteria. Item 7 HIGH: no coder count, no reliability statistic, no validated instrument. Item 9 LOW: 21 July - 31 August 2020 window stated and justified. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 120 top-shared articles, so the headline 'no misinformation on social media' claim rests on a 120-item curated head of the distribution.

quote_item6: Article content data were mapped against this timeline to see if Indian media reporting adapted to new information, and whether the content was accurate.
quote_item10: Three hundred and fourteen articles discussed COVID-19 treatments.
notes: Item 6 HIGH: there is no explicit misinformation case definition anywhere in the paper; 'misleading' is judged narratively against a WHO-updates timeline within the WHO Strategic Communications Framework, which is a communication-effectiveness instrument (actionable/credible/understandable/relevant/timely), not a falsity standard. Contrast with 85127039075, which also used WHO/CDC but checked discrete factual statements against it - here the construct is guideline concordance of evolving treatment coverage (plasma therapy, chloroquine). Item 7 HIGH: four coders splitting the corpus, discrepancies discussed daily, but no kappa and no validated coding instrument. Item 3 LOW: census of the dedicated 'Coronavirus' sections of the five newspapers over the date range (3507 screened -> 2422 included). Item 9 LOW: 11 March - 30 April 2020 stated. Item 10 HIGH: the 40% headline is over 314 treatment-discussing articles, a subset of 2422 COVID articles, and the 40% is asserted in the abstract without a traceable numerator in the Results.

quote_item6: while misleading sources are defined as ones that contain “misleading content, false and/or hyper-partisan news as well as hoaxes, conspiracy theories, click-bait and satire.”
quote_item10: Only 3% of the posts with hyperlinks in them contained links to either the professional news or misleading sources in our study: the majority linked to other websites, mostly in other languages such as Farsi, Russian and Arabic.
notes: Methodologically the most careful study in the shard, and it still fails on the two load-bearing items - a good illustration of the review's argument. Item 1 LOW: target population is English-language public Telegram channels, a real venue not defined by the outcome. Item 2 HIGH: snowball-crawled frame seeded from 250 channels, which the authors candidly flag as non-comprehensive. Item 3 LOW: complete trace of all 24.7M messages in the frame over the year. Item 7 LOW: the Pierri et al. source list is externally maintained since 2016 and reused across published studies (Grinberg et al., Shao et al.). Item 9 LOW: full year, 1 Oct 2018 - 30 Sep 2019. Item 6 HIGH: the domain list bundles hyper-partisan news, click-bait and satire with falsity, so quality/partisanship stands in for the falsity construct (the authors did strip humour/parody sites, reducing the list to 94). Item 10 HIGH and severe: the 37.5-38% figure has as its denominator only the 202,571 posts that linked to one of the two curated lists, which is 3% of hyperlinked posts and a far smaller fraction of all posts - a doubly-curated denominator presented as platform prevalence.

quote_item6: We built a list of ‘subthemes’ by reviewing the publicly available materials from three vaccine-focused organisations (Planned Parenthood, the Adult Vaccine Access Coalition and the Immunisation Action Coalition).
quote_item10: 41 718 (3.2% of all COVID-19 vaccine articles) contained at least one of the vaccine misinformation themes based on the Boolean string developed for this study.
notes: Census of all COVID-19 vaccine articles in 100 highest-reach English-language outlets (items 1-3 LOW). Content-only design: items 4-5 NA. Item 6 LOW: subthemes drawn from external vaccine organisations and the headline 0.1% figure is close-read validated (primary misinformation vs fact-checking vs refers-to). Bracketed reference markers stripped from the item-6 quote.

quote_item6: To create this list we consulted diﬀerent sources e.g. The WHO Mythbusters resource2, the COVID19MisInfo.org3 portal [16] and similar lists created by Islam et al. [17] and Evanega et al. [12].

ITEM-6 RULING APPLIED in spirit: the misinformation theme list is anchored to external, pre-existing sources (WHO Mythbusters, COVID19MisInfo.org, Islam et al., Evanega et al.) rather than being author-invented -> item 6 LOW. Item 7 is a clear LOW and the best in this shard: two coders on 2,000 queries with Cohen's kappa = 0.946, and the deployed classifier reports ROC-AUC >96% and sensitivity >90%. Item 2 HIGH: the frame is Microsoft's curated desktop-only 'coronavirus intent' query set (intent partly inferred by random walks on the click graph), yet the framing generalises to 'how widespread the interest in misinformation topics among US citizens is'. Item 4 HIGH: no treatment of who is and is not a desktop Bing user. quote_item6: The questionnaire collected information regarding sociodemographics, means used to clarify doubts about health, implementation of information obtained through the Internet, receipt of fake news, and means of transmission of fake news.

notes: Abstract only. Item 6 HIGH: purely self-reported 'receipt of fake news' with no external ground truth and no definition given to respondents in anything we can see - respondent-devised, not merely author-devised. Item 7 HIGH: no validation or reliability for the instrument. Items 2-4 HIGH: snowball recruitment through social media platforms gives no defined sampling frame and no computable response rate, and self-selection is not addressed. Item 9 HIGH: no recall window at all ('had received fake news' is effectively lifetime), which is a large part of why the figure is 89.4%. Item 10 is LOW on its own terms - the denominator is the 1,195 respondents, a real (if badly recruited) audience - so the study is HIGH by the >=6-HIGH clause rather than the 6+10 clause.

quote_item6: Next, we assessed whether the claims made in the article titles contained misinformation through comparative analyses with evidence-based and reputable sources (i.e., government agencies, international organizations, and peer-reviewed scientific literature).
quote_item10: A total of 114 article links shared through tweets were assessed for health misinformation. In total, 30 news articles (26.3%) contained misinformation.
notes: Khamar et al. Item 6 HIGH: no external list and no fact-check verdicts - the authors themselves judged article TITLES against an unspecified set of 'reputable sources', which is internal and ad hoc; they also concede that 20 of 114 titles 'could not be assessed based on the title alone', so the numerator is unstable. Item 7 HIGH and explicit: 'Inter-rater reliability was not assessed in this study.' Items 1-3 HIGH: BuzzSumo top-10-most-shared articles per topic per window is simultaneously keyword-seeded, topic-curated and top-N-by-engagement. Item 10 HIGH: 114 curated top-shared articles across three hand-picked COVID topics is not any audience's diet, yet the result is reported as 'the prevalence of misinformation on Twitter'. Items 4-5 NA (content analysis).

quote_item6: We followed three fact-checking portals in Serbia - Istinomer, AFP Fact Check, and Fake News Tragac - and on the basis of their work we formed a database of 25 fact-checked and debunked claims.

Item 10 LOW: population denominator (800 adults 18-74, interlocked quotas by sex/age/region, MoE +/-3.5%) - the population-denominator design the review treats as appropriate. Item 2 HIGH on the authors' own admission that the online-only self-administered frame excludes people without internet access and omits education quotas; item 3 HIGH (quota, not probability, sampling); item 4 UNCLEAR (no response/attrition rate reported for the panel); item 7 HIGH - single binary 'Have you heard about this topic before?' with no validation and, as the authors state, no placebo narrative to bound false recall (they cite 14% false recall in Allcott & Gentzkow); item 9 HIGH - the recall item specifies no time window.

quote_item6: NO QUOTE FOUND

Denominator is high-engagement ('popular') melanoma media articles - a curated topical, engagement-selected corpus -> items 1-3 HIGH, item 10 HIGH. No definition, reliability statistic or observation window recoverable -> items 6-9 UNCLEAR. Overall HIGH follows from item 10 HIGH plus item 6 UNCLEAR treated as HIGH (checklist line 47); abstract-only sensitivity candidate.

quote_item6: Videos were operationally classified as containing "aligned information" when at least one evaluated recommendation aligned with an official oral hygiene protocol.
quote_item10: Overall, 26.19% aligned with at least one protocol, while 73.81% contained unsupported or non-aligned information
notes: 246 Spanish-language TikTok oral-hygiene videos from 11 hashtags, May-Jul 2025, collected on a fresh no-history account. Item 3 LOW (all retrieved videos screened against stated eligibility criteria rather than top-N by engagement) and item 7 LOW (two calibrated evaluators, Cohen's kappa = 0.86, triple-blinded, third-reviewer adjudication) - methodologically careful. But items 1-2 HIGH: hashtag-seeded topical corpus, and eligibility explicitly excluded videos 'promoted home remedies or pseudotherapies', removing a misinformation-dense stratum. Item 6 HIGH under the checklist's explicit exclusion: non-alignment with FDI/ADA/FOE/FDE clinical protocols is guideline adherence standing in for falsity, not an external falsity standard (coded QUALITY in the extraction). Item 10 HIGH: 73.81% is a share of a curated 246-video topical corpus, presented as misinformation prevalence.

quote_item6: The facticity of the content was evaluated against current scientific evidence, including guidelines, consensus statements, and systematic reviews related to dental caries management.
quote_item10: To select the 500 most relevant posts based on total interaction, two independent investigators conducted a manual assessment, ensuring that only posts meeting the inclusion criteria were selected.
notes: Content analysis (items 4/5 NA). Item 6 LOW: falsity judged against an external, pre-existing standard (published caries guidelines/consensus statements/systematic reviews), with an explicit falsity threshold ('a post was considered to contain misinformation only if it unequivocally presented false or misleading information'). Item 7 LOW: two calibrated coders, ICC 0.84-0.96 reported. Item 3 HIGH: top-N by total interaction out of 21,210 retrieved posts. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 500 highest-engagement Portuguese caries posts, not any audience's diet.

quote_item6: Posts that included any content that could be easily be rebutted using any of the aforementioned sites were considered misinformation while we categorized unverifiable information as posts that could not be proven either correct or incorrect by the same sources.

notes: Content analysis (items 4/5 NA). Item 6 LOW: external, pre-existing anchor (WHO/CDC guidance used as a refutation standard for falsity, not as a quality rubric). Item 7 HIGH: no coder-reliability statistic and no validated instrument. Item 9 HIGH: three-day search window (14-16 July 2020) with no content date range. Item 10 HIGH and internally inconsistent: 146/454 = 32.2%, not the reported 22.3%; account-type percentages are likewise not fractions of 454 (291 verified reported as 44.5%), so the stated denominator does not reproduce the reported numbers. Frame further restricted to English posts with >=10 likes.

quote_item6: NO QUOTE FOUND
quote_item10: From the 72 videos selected, about 40 (55.5%) of them had misleading information and about 32 (44.5%) of them had useful information
notes: No cached full text (text_path empty; not present in data/abstracts) - rated from the abstract-level record only. Item 6 UNCLEAR: no verbatim case definition available; the only reported dichotomy is 'misleading' vs 'useful', which conflates falsity with usefulness/quality, but no quote could be verified, so UNCLEAR per protocol (treated as HIGH in the overall). Item 7 UNCLEAR: two coders mentioned, no reliability statistic retrievable. Item 9 UNCLEAR: no observation window reported. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 72 videos from the first three pages of oral-health keyword searches; n_high counts affirmative HIGHs only.

quote_item6: Twenty-five videos claimed that chiropractic manipulation could "fix" the Eustachian tube, and 14 videos (28%) asserted nerve correction; none mentioned antibiotics or tympanostomy tubes.
quote_item10: Twenty-five videos claimed that chiropractic manipulation could "fix" the Eustachian tube, and 14 videos (28%) asserted nerve correction; none mentioned antibiotics or tympanostomy tubes.

Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 50 keyword-retrieved YouTube videos; the two reported percentages (50%, 28%) are shares of a curated topical video set presented as prevalence. Items 6 and 10 both HIGH -> overall HIGH.

quote_item6: Videos were classified as containing disinformation/misinformation if they contained information in contradiction to clinical recommendations.
quote_item10: A total of 677 videos were analyzed (2016-2025). After exclusion criteria, 563 videos remained, 167 from TikTok, 196 from Instagram Reels and 200 from YouTube Shorts.
notes: Content analysis (items 4/5 NA). Item 6 HIGH under the explicit v3 exception: contradiction with clinical recommendations is guideline-adherence standing in for falsity, applied by the authors' own three evaluators with no external ground truth (no fact-check verdicts, no credibility list); the source-level-list ruling does not apply because no external list is used. Item 7 LOW: interrater agreement 83.5% (95% CI 80.6-86.0) reported. Item 3 HIGH: 250 algorithm-ranked native-search results per platform. Item 9 LOW: content span 2016-2025 stated (single-day retrieval, 8 June 2025). Items 6 and 10 both HIGH -> overall HIGH.

quote_item6: We gathered a database of fake news articles that circulated in the three months before the 2016 election, using lists from three independent third parties.

notes: Item 6 LOW: external, pre-existing fact-check ground truth (Snopes, PolitiFact, BuzzFeed lists) plus a published 65-site fake-news domain list. Item 7 LOW: placebo-headline design explicitly validates the recall measure against false recall. Item 3 HIGH: SurveyMonkey Audience opt-in panel, not probability sampling (reweighted to national margins). Item 4 UNCLEAR: no response or completion rate reported. Item 5 HIGH: the survey estimates are direct from subjects, but the headline exposure share (5%) and per-adult impression counts are derived from Alexa aggregate traffic, i.e. an inferred rather than observed audience. Item 10 LOW: denominators are all US adults and total news-site impressions - whole-diet/defined totals, not a curated misinformation subset. Strongest study in the shard.

quote_item6: Lastly, we used in this study an algorithm developed by Storyzy in order to sort the selected information sources into two categories: "reliable" and "unreliable."
quote_item10: Among all participants, 5% of connected time dedicated to information was spent consulting information sources considered to be unreliable, which equates to 0.16% of total connected time
notes: Item 6 LOW under the source-level-list ruling: Storyzy is a third-party, pre-existing source-level reliability classification (30,000+ sources), externally anchored and cross-checked against Le Monde's Decodex-style classification; source-level identification is recorded separately in classification_level/breadth and is not penalised twice here. Item 3 LOW: complete 30-day behavioural trace of the whole panel. Item 4 HIGH: 52% of panel members refused or could not be tracked on mobile, a large coverage gap for news consumption that is described but not adjusted for. Item 7 HIGH: Storyzy's classifier accuracy is never quantified (no precision/recall, only a qualitative comparison with Le Monde). Item 10 LOW: denominators are total connected time and total information time for a panel representative of French adults 18+ - the whole-diet denominator this review treats as appropriate.

quote_item6: A critical advantage of our study is that we use the for-sure fake articles from Rick Pearson and the SEC to validate the linguistic algorithm and calibrate the authenticity score into a probability of fake news.
quote_item10: The unconditional probability of a Seeking Alpha article being fake is 2.8% over the entire sample period, peaking at 4.8% in 2008 and dropping to a low of 1.6% in 2013
notes: Content analysis (items 4/5 NA). Item 6 LOW: ground truth is 171 SEC-prosecuted 'for-sure fake' promotional articles - external, pre-existing and legally adjudicated - used to calibrate the LIWC authenticity classifier. Item 7 LOW: classifier validated out of sample against the SEC set with type I/II error rates reported, though it is deliberately conservative (137 of 171 known fakes go unclassified), so 2.8% is a lower bound. Item 3 LOW: complete census of all 203,545 articles 2005-2015. Item 1 HIGH: a single niche investor-commentary platform is not a general audience/national population. Item 10 LOW: denominator is the complete article corpus of the platform - a defined total, not a curated topical subset - but note this is platform content share, not audience exposure.

quote_item6: Tweets that included information that could be clearly refuted using one of the above-mentioned references were considered under misinformation.
quote_item10: Our search was limited to tweets in the English language and to those that initially received at least five retweets. We excluded tweets that had four or fewer retweets.
notes: Content analysis (items 4/5 NA). Item 6 LOW: external, pre-existing refutation standard (WHO, CDC, peer-reviewed journals) applied as a falsity test, not a quality rubric. Item 3 LOW: 50 tweets per search term drawn by computer-generated random sequences. Item 2 HIGH: frame is 14 trending COVID hashtags/keywords filtered to >=5 retweets - engagement-thresholded and topic-curated. Item 7 HIGH: no reliability statistic and no validated instrument. Item 9 HIGH: single-day retrieval (27 February 2020) generalised to 'the magnitude of misinformation'. Item 10 HIGH: 24.8% is a share of a curated, retweet-filtered topical tweet set. 5 affirmative HIGHs with item 6 LOW -> MODERATE.

quote_item6: We adopt three lists of "fake news" sites as proposed in [14]: black sites, orange sites, red sites.
quote_item10: It is likely that there are more tweets discussing these stories, than listed here, as selection on keyword tends to under-sample.
notes: Item 6 LOW under the source-level-list ruling: the Grinberg et al. black/red/orange domain lists are a published third-party source-level credibility list; the fact that they key on 'lack of editorial norms' rather than verified falsity is captured by the breadth moderator (unreliable_source), not penalised here. Item 3 LOW: complete filtered-stream capture of the keyword corpus (67.4M tweets, 12.0M users). Item 5 LOW: user-level behavioural trace. Item 7 LOW: external published list plus user classifiers with reported accuracies (country 92.96%, identity 95.4%, political orientation 87.4%). Item 2 HIGH: seven COVID keywords define the frame, which the authors themselves note under-samples. Item 10 HIGH: the 1.60%/2.50% reach figures are denominated on users who tweeted with COVID keywords in a five-week window, not on a general population or a whole diet, and the 82.45% figure is denominated on fake-news sharers themselves. Item 10 HIGH with item 6 LOW -> MODERATE.

quote_item6: After a thorough review of existing literature, the videos were classified into four non-overlapping groups: Informative-content that conveys medically correct information about one or more aspects of the disease including epidemiology, prevention, clinical features, screening and testing and treatment to its viewers; Misleading-content that is scientifically inaccurate or makes ambiguous claims that are not evidence-based

Items 1-3 HIGH: top-120 keyword search results per language, first 40 retained -> curated topical corpus, purposive top-N. Item 7 LOW: kappa reported per language, two independent reviewers. Item 9 HIGH: single-day snapshot (8 April 2020) generalised to prevalence. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 240 search-returned videos, not any audience's diet.

quote_item6: Content categories were created using a fact sheet from the CDC and our prior study on YouTube and COVID-19 vaccines. ... Further content categories included if the video highlighted any of the following: the false claim that a vaccine was available for uptake (at the time the data was collected, it was not available in the US)
quote_item10: One-hundred trending videos were identified from the hashtag #covidvaccine. At the time of the study, this was the most popular of the COVID-19 hashtags with approximately 73.8 million views.
notes: Item 6 LOW: the falsity claim is anchored to an external, verifiable fact (no US vaccine was publicly available at the time) with categories built from a CDC fact sheet - external and pre-existing, not author-devised subjective coding. Items 1-3 HIGH: 100 trending videos from a single hashtag, selected on popularity. Item 7 LOW: double-coding of a 10% random sample, kappa = .94. Item 9 HIGH: single undated snapshot of 'trending' content. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 100 trending hashtag videos; the 31% figure is a share of a curated topical sample, not audience exposure.

quote_item6: Benefits, efficacy, costs, safety, adverse effects, contraindications and precautions, dosage, target groups for vaccination, and myths and conspiracy theories were also recorded.
quote_item10: After applying the exclusion criteria (not available for viewing, language other than Spanish, videos that were duplicated, and videos that did not provide information on Covid-19 vaccines), the 118 most widely viewed videos were selected.
notes: Item 6 HIGH: 'hoaxes and conspiracy theories' are identified by the two authors with no external list, fact-check verdict or stated criterion; the only externally borrowed scheme is the message-tone classification, which is sentiment, not falsity. Items 1-3 HIGH: three keyword searches sorted by view count, top 118 retained. Item 7 LOW: two independent raters, kappa = 0.971 (reported for message tone; hoax-specific reliability not given - borderline). Item 9 HIGH: single-day search (9 February 2021). Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 118 most-viewed topical videos.

quote_item6: The fake news classifications were based on Grinberg et al, which has a three tier classification system for fake news domains: orange, red and black. Here we classify “black” and “red” domains as fake
quote_item10: Of the 29,662,169 COVID-19 tweets in our panel, 7,062,989 contained at least one URL. ... URLs from domains that publish fake news only comprise 1.1% of the URLs from COVID-19 tweets
notes: Item 6 LOW: Grinberg/Lazer black-red-orange domain lists, named explicitly in the ruling. Strong external validity otherwise: 1.6M registered-voter panel matched to Twitter, complete behavioural trace, 9-month window, published sensitivity to the orange tier. Item 4 LOW: passive trace of a matched voter panel, so non-response is not the operative bias. Item 10 HIGH: the denominator is COVID-19 tweets containing a URL, a topical subset of a topical subset - the 1.1% is a share of COVID URL-sharing, not of these users' whole information diet. Sole HIGH, but it is item 10, so MODERATE by the pre-specified weighting.

quote_item6: each tweet was selected for its connection to one of 456 misinformation stories — distinct stories that included false, exaggerated, unsubstantiated or otherwise misleading claims ... These stories were (1) first identified through a collaborative reporting process as part of the Election Integrity Partnership
quote_item10: The top 35 accounts alone were responsible for 9,304,879 out of 32,581,921—or 28.6%—of all “sows doubt” connected retweets and quote tweets we collected.
notes: Item 6 HIGH: the case definition is the authors' own real-time EIP curation - internal and ad hoc rather than external and pre-existing - and the inclusion criterion explicitly extends to 'exaggerated, unsubstantiated or otherwise misleading' claims with no requirement of a fact-check verdict. This is NOT a source-level credibility list, so the ruling does not apply. Item 1 HIGH: the universe is accounts spreading the curated misinformation stories (selection on the outcome). Item 2 HIGH: 456 bespoke boolean search strings over a keyword-seeded election stream. Item 7 LOW: two coders per story, Fleiss kappa = 0.64, third-coder arbitration. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 32.6M 'sows doubt' retweets, i.e. the misinformation set itself; the concentration figure is share-of-misinformation, not share-of-diet. Both 6 and 10 HIGH -> HIGH overall despite excellent execution within its own frame.

quote_item6: NewsGuard employs a team of journalists and editors to rate news outlets from 0 to 100 based on nine journalistic norms of credibility and transparency, including whether they publish false content and/or use deceptive headlines ... NewsGuard categorizes news outlets with a score of 60 or lower as “generally untrustworthy” and above 60 as “generally trustworthy”.
quote_item10: Web traffic refers to the total number of visits to news websites, whereas Facebook engagement to the number of likes, emojis, shares, and comments, accumulated on the posts of news outlets’ Facebook pages. In 2020, generally untrustworthy news outlets, as rated by NewsGuard, accounted for 2.28% of the web traffic to news outlets and 13.97% of the Facebook engagement with news outlets.
notes: Item 6 LOW UNDER THE RULING: NewsGuard is named explicitly; the score-<=60 cut is a credibility-not-falsity standard, but the strict 'repeatedly publishes false content' variant is also reported. Item 10 LOW: the denominator is a defined total (all Comscore-measured news traffic / all news-page Facebook engagement) and matches the claim the paper actually makes; it is not selected on misinformation. Item 5 HIGH: the Facebook half of the estimates is publisher-side aggregate engagement on outlets' own pages, not audience-level trace - the authors flag this themselves; the Comscore web-traffic half is a genuine behavioural panel. Item 4 UNCLEAR: Comscore panel recruitment, opt-in and attrition are not discussed. Cleanest study in the shard.

quote_item6: To collect false stories circulating across Brazil from 2018 to 2020, we scraped fact-checked stories from the six main fact-checking agencies in Brazil (Boatos, E-farsas, Fato ou Fake, Lupa, Aos Fatos, and Projeto Comprova).
quote_item10: Using our text-based approach, about 0.01% (421) of politicians’ posts contain false stories ... we collected just over 4 million social media posts (1.5 million from Facebook, 1.1 million from Instagram and 1.5 million from Twitter).
notes: Item 6 LOW: fact-checker verdicts (Boatos corpus, cross-validated against five other Brazilian agencies) for the text approach and a fact-check-flagged domain list for the domain approach - both external and pre-existing. Item 1 HIGH: the population is 945 elite politicians, i.e. producers, not an audience or the national public. Item 2-3 LOW: complete census of a comprehensive handle list across three platforms. Item 7 LOW: F1 .926-.954, per-platform models, two Portuguese-speaking coders plus third-coder adjudication, disagreement rate reported. Item 10 LOW: denominator is all 4.03M posts by those politicians - a complete, uncurated total that matches the claim. Only weakness is that the unit is producer output rather than audience exposure.

quote_item6: use the term “misinformation” to label content in news media that is at variance with generally-accepted scientific facts on the GMO issue, as discussed above.
quote_item10: Our search string returned 535 relevant articles, which were then categorized into 5 topics ... Overall, about 9% of the articles published on GMOs from 2019–2021 that we reviewed contained misinformation, while 91% were factually accurate
notes: Item 6 LOW: falsity is anchored to a documented external standard (published meta-analyses and expert consensus on GM safety, cited at length) rather than to author taste - the same category as 'expert-verified false claims'. Judgement call: the operational rule ('without qualification or rebuttal') is applied by the authors alone, with no external adjudicator, no double coding and no reliability statistic (item 7), so this is the least secure item-6 LOW in the shard. Items 1-2 HIGH: Boolean keyword search over a pre-set outlet list, with African outlets deliberately added. Item 7 HIGH: no double coding, no reliability statistic. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 535 GMO-topic articles; worse for the regional figures, since the authors state the African media list was intentionally oversampled, so the 20% Africa estimate rests on a denominator the paper itself describes as deliberately oversampled.

quote_item6: conspiracy narratives are beliefs and convictions that attempt to interpret historical and contemporary events and general societal changes as a conspiracy and/or secret plan by a group of powerful actors ... A message is annotated as showing signs of conspiracy (annotated as 1) if it clearly indicates signs of conspiracy narratives
quote_item10: Resulting in a corpus of 821,903 messages that were exchanged in 34 groups. ... our trained model identified 67,698 messages containing characteristics of conspiracy narratives, representing 8.24% of the total corpus
notes: Item 6 HIGH: the target is 'signs of conspiracy narratives' judged against author-written annotation guidelines; the cited conceptual definition (Pigden, Keeley) is a scholarly construct, not an external falsity standard, and no claim is checked against any verdict or list. Not a source-level credibility list, so the ruling does not apply. Item 1 HIGH: the population is 34 Querdenken anti-lockdown protest chat groups - selection on exactly the phenomenon measured. Items 2-3 LOW: all public groups advertised by the main initiative, complete message census. Item 7 LOW: four expert annotators, kappa = 0.82, DistilBERT macro F1 = .851 (but only .757 for the positive class). Item 9 LOW: 25-month window. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is the movement's own chat corpus, which no audience-level prevalence claim can rest on.

quote_item6: In this study, misinformation is defined as any false, inaccurate, or conspiratorial information pertaining to COVID-19 and vaccination. ... Our annotation training adhered to the COVID-19 misinformation codebook by Memon and Carley (2020), a model for subsequent studies (Moffitt et al., 2021).
quote_item10: Similarly, the misinformation classification model identifies 460,087 tweets as misinformation, accounting for over 27% of the dataset.
notes: Item 6 LOW: external pre-existing published codebook (Memon & Carley 2020) plus consultation of fact-checking sites = external anchor. Items 1-2 HIGH: universe is a 147-keyword Finnish vaccine-tweet corpus, not an audience; authors concede Twitter's 'lack of representativeness of the general population'. Item 3 LOW: full census of the keyword frame. Item 7 HIGH: misinformation classifier F1 = 0.67 (accuracy 0.85) and the classifier-labelled rate (27%) is ~1.6x the human-annotated rate in the training sample (709/4150 = 17%), so the instrument is not shown valid at the prevalence claim it supports; Krippendorff's alpha 0.668 is only 'good' by the authors' own cut-offs. Item 9 LOW: Dec 2019-Oct 2022 stated. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is a topical keyword corpus, reported as 'Approximately a third of tweets contained misinformation'.

quote_item6: I, therefore, use misinformation as an umbrella term, following Sanaullah et al. [19], defining it as any information that is incorrect, misleading, or false, regardless of the intent of the disseminator.
quote_item10: This results in a final dataset of 426,262 binary classified tweets, with a proportion of 5.11% being classified as containing misinformation.
notes: Item 6 HIGH: adopting another paper's CONCEPTUAL definition is not an external ground truth; operationalisation is an author-written codebook (Appendix 1) applied to 994 tweets with no fact-check verdicts, credibility list or external verification behind it - internal and ad hoc under the ruling. Items 1-2 HIGH: Norwegian COVID-keyword tweet corpus, not an audience. Item 3 LOW: census of the keyword frame. Item 7 LOW: kappa 0.78 between two annotators, third-annotator adjudication, plus a blind 300-tweet validation of the classifier (kappa 0.791). Item 10 HIGH: topical keyword denominator; the CONCENTRATION estimate (25% of users = 75% of misinfo) has a denominator restricted to misinformation-posting users. Both 6 and 10 HIGH -> overall HIGH. Note the self-training pipeline dumps 130,065 unpredictable tweets into the non-misinformation class, a stated false-negative risk.

quote_item6: This study employed two data sources: subtitles from ten German public broadcast news or talk shows between June 2023 and June 2024 (n = 1382) and checked claims in articles from six German fact-checking organizations between January 2023 and June 2024 (n = 462).
quote_item10: It finds 77 matches in 67 episodes, amounting to 4.85% of the 1382 episodes during the sampling period between June 2023 and June 2024.
notes: Strongest study in this shard. Item 6 LOW: case definition is external fact-check verdicts from six German organisations (four of them IFCN signatories, three in Meta's 3PFC). Items 1-3 LOW: near-census of all 1382 episodes of the ten most-watched German public-broadcast news and talk shows over 12 months - a real, large audience, no selection on the outcome. Items 4-5 NA (content analysis of broadcast supply). Item 7 LOW: retrieval pipeline validated (ChatGPT matching F1 = 84.21%; false-negative rate estimated at 14% against a hand-built benchmark) with three student annotators validating candidate pairs; the single-expert step covers descriptive categories (speaker, deception type), not the prevalence numerator. Item 10 LOW: denominator is the full episode population, not a curated subset. Caveat recorded, not scored: the numerator is a lower bound because only claims a fact-checker had already checked can match - the author states 'This biased selection renders the study exploratory in nature rather than representative.'

quote_item6: To evaluate the presence of incorrect information, the content was analysed by comparing the claims made with information on PubMed, in medical literature, or other reliable sources like medical journals.
quote_item10: Sixty-eight percent of 121 posts did not present any misinformation. Thirty-two percent of videos contained some form of medically related misinformation.
notes: Item 6 LOW: falsity anchored to external, pre-existing peer-reviewed medical evidence (PubMed / medical journals) rather than author opinion - the 'expert-verified false claims' route; the DISCERN-style quality-instrument failure mode does not apply here. quote_item6: Following best practice for source-based research on misinformation and news trustworthiness (Lin et al., 2023; Luhring et al., 2024), we used NewsGuard-an established database for source-based news credibility labels rated according to apolitical journalistic standards-to classify websites as trustworthy or untrustworthy. ... Sources are considered untrustworthy if the score is below 60 on a 0-100 scale.
quote_item10: We focus on two individual-level measures of exposure: the share of visits to untrustworthy news outlets among all news visits-in the raw data 0.75% in 2017 and 0.52% in 2024-and the average NewsGuard score (ranging from 0-lowest to 100-highest reliability) across all news visits, in the raw data, stable at 96 in both years.
notes: Item 6 LOW: NewsGuard is a published source-level credibility list - LOW on its own merits and squarely inside the 2026-07-23 ruling. Items 1-3 LOW: German adults from the YouGov Pulse panel, 2017 wave quota-matched to the online population and matching the actual AfD vote share (13.9% vs 12.6%); complete passive behavioural trace (56M URL visits) rather than a sample of visits. Item 4 LOW: opt-in/coverage bias explicitly addressed - the 2024 wave's AfD underrepresentation is quantified against the 2025 election and the authors state their 'estimates likely understate actual levels of exposure'; response/attrition rates themselves are not reported. Item 5 LOW: passive metering of the subjects' own browsing. Item 7 LOW: NewsGuard validated externally (Lin et al. 2023 correspondence across rating sets) and results robust to score thresholds of 50 and 70. Item 8 LOW: 2017 desktop-only vs 2024 desktop+mobile, but a desktop-only robustness specification is run. Item 9 LOW: 6-month (2017) and 2-month (2024) windows stated, and the authors explicitly flag that the binary reach indicator is window-sensitive. Item 10 LOW: denominators are all news visits and all participants - a real audience's whole news diet. Only the two CONCENTRATION estimates use a within-untrustworthy denominator, which is correct for a concentration measure.

notes: Item 6 HIGH: the case definition is a project-specific, iteratively developed coding frame built from the authors' own 'public health perspective' - critique-of-sunscreen as a proxy for falsity, with no fact-check verdicts, credibility list or independent expert adjudication; the authors explicitly did not verify individual product claims ('Analysis was not conducted on each individual product profiled to determine whether a product with low SPF was inaccurately promoted'). Item1/2 LOW: a real national adult population reached through a panel explicitly balanced to represent it. Item3 HIGH: quota balancing on an opt-in commercial panel, not probability selection. notes: Sen, Jeswin, Bellary & Sai Kumar, Journal of Community Health Management 2023. quote_item6: content from misinformation repeat offenders (sources identified by Facebook as repeatedly posting misinformation)

notes: Nyhan et al., Nature 2023 (US 2020 Facebook and Instagram Election Study). Field experiment with 23,377 consenting US Facebook users, Feed exposures logged 24 September - 23 December 2020; the 0.76% is the control group's Feed. Item1 LOW: the target population is US adult monthly-active Facebook users, with survey weights built to that population and benchmarked against an AmeriSpeak probability sample. Item2 LOW: recruitment was by survey invitation placed in the Feeds of eligible users platform-wide. Item3 LOW: the exposure measure is a complete platform-side behavioural trace of every Feed view, not a sample of content. Item4 HIGH: participation required consent to an in-Feed invitation and the authors state plainly that participants 'use Facebook more frequently than the general Facebook population and are exposed to more content from politically like-minded sources (the phenomenon of interest)'; weights are applied to the attitudinal PATEs, not to this descriptive exposure share, so the selection runs in the same direction as the quantity being estimated. Item5 LOW: trace from the subjects' own accounts. Item6 LOW: the case definition is Meta's repeat-misinformation-offender source designation - external to the researchers and pre-existing, which is what the source-level ruling requires; it is proprietary and unauditable, and that is charged at item7 rather than counted twice here. Item10 LOW: the denominator is ALL Feed content exposures of the control group - a real audience's entire received diet - which is exactly what the item asks for. Recorded as source-level under addendum H: this is the share of exposures FROM flagged sources, not the share of exposures that were false. This and W4414259328/scholar_01 are the two population-scale trace studies in the batch and the instrument separates them from the small surveys cleanly, with items 6 and 10 both LOW.
